newsitem.title: FRANCE: Le Pen says Chirac's Europe is Hitler's dream.
newsitem.headline: Le Pen says Chirac's Europe is Hitler's dream.

text.p: French Socialists on Thursday sought to distance themselves from the far-right, whose leader Jean-Marie Le Pen urged a leftist parliamentary election victory to thwart plans for Europe that he said would make "Hitler's dream come true".

Le Pen urged supporters to back leftists in the election run-off in constituencies where his National Front candidates do not survive the first-round ballot in order to block President Jacques Chirac's plans to take France into the single currency.
"This sort of Europe, dominated by Germany and organised in 'Laender'-like provinces ignoring existing nations, will make Hitler's dream come true," Le Pen told the daily Le Parisien.
He said a leftist victory in the May 25-June 1 election would help his cause by paralysing the country and blocking its drift towards European integration including a single currency.
Socialist Party leader Lionel Jospin hastened to warn the right against trying to use Le Pen's words against the left.

"If anything has to be clarified, it is on the side of the right...If there is any leakage, it is between the ideas of the far-right and the right, never with the left's ideas," he told a Paris youth rally.
He recalled that the National Front's number two, Bruno Megret was a former Gaullist and the Gaullist mayor of Nice, Jacques Peyrat, was a former National Front member.

Piqued by Prime Minister Alain Juppe's assertion that the opposition was "an eccentric coalition" ranging from the Communists to the National Front, he accused centrist Urban Affairs Minister Jean-Claude Gaudin and ex-defence minister Francois Leotard of making election deals with the Front.

Le Pen told Radio Luxembourg that forcing the conservative head of state to share power with a leftist government "would tie Chirac's hands on Europe, and will lead to a new dissolution within a year".
Perhaps the next time round, the National Front "will be better placed to win power than it is now", he said.
An Ipsos opinion poll said the ruling centre-right would win a clear majority with 323 seats -- up from 290 a week ago -- to the combined left's 293.
While the Front itself was seen wining only one of 577 seats in the National Assembly, pollsters say its supporters are in a position to play a decisive role in the run-off.
Yet polls find that Front voters, who make up 13 percent to 15 percent of the total, look set to ignore Le Pen's advice and prefer conservatives over Socialists or Communists in run-offs.
Jospin told the Paris rally developments in Zaire, where President Mobutu Sese Seko faces a rebel onslaught, sealed "the failure of French African policy".
"What is happening in Zaire today seals the failure of Chirac's policy which put Mobutu back in the saddle," he said, adding that rebel Laurent Kabila could be another dictator.
Jospin also took Chirac to task for using his election motto "A New Impulse" in a speech to businessmen partly broadcast on French television during his current state visit to China.

"I heard him using the...slogan to Chinese masses who must have been taken aback. It is not usual practice to speak of domestic politics abroad, especially in the midst of an election campaign," Jospin said.

Unpopular Gaullist Prime Minister Alain Juppe, campaigning in his hometown Bordeaux, acknowledged discontent over record unemployment but warned disgruntled conservatives against being tempted to cast protest votes in the first round and go fishing instead of voting in the run-off.
"Such behaviour, get this well into your head, could return Socialism to power," he said.
Chirac has urged the right to stop squabbling after allies of Juppe accused him of dragging down the government campaign and hinted he should be replaced if the right wins the election.
Aides said Juppe "had not ruled out succeeding himself".

In social unrest, farmers dumped tonnes of fruit and vegetables in several cities to protest at low-price foreign produce, and 200 protesters briefly occupied the Bank of France, accusing it of causing poverty with its free-market policies.

Train controllers worried about job cuts and bonuses threatened to prolong a strike restricting rail traffic across the country, and pilots at state-owned Air France and Air France Europe said they would walk out for four days beginning next Tuesday in a dispute over wages and working conditions.
